parole.significato: algebra (a system for computation using letters or other symbols to represent numbers, with rules for manipulating thes…
parole.testo: Internationalism, from Medieval Latin algebra, from Arabic الْجَبْر (al-jabr). First attested in c. 1708–1710.
From Medieval Latin alchymia, from Arabic اَلْكِيمِيَاء (al-kīmiyāʔ, “alchemy”).

Borrowed from Medieval Latin amalgama (“amalgam”), from Arabic اَلْمَلْغَم (al-malḡam, “softening ointment, emollient poultice; amalgam”), from Ancient Greek μάλαγμᾰ (málagmă, “emollient”), from μᾰλάσσω (mălássō, “to soften”), from μᾰλᾰκός (mălăkós, “soft”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin cifra (“zero, numeral”), from Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr, “zero, empty, nothing”).
From Medieval Latin chimia, from Arabic الكِيمِيَاء (al-kīmiyāʔ). First attested in 1728.

parole.significato: glaze (transparent or semi-transparent layer of paint)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin lazur (“lapis lazuli; azure”), from Arabic لَازُوَرْد (lāzuward, “lapis lazuli; azure”), from Persian لاجورد (lâjvard, “lapis lazuli; azure”). Compare German Lasur (“glaze”).
From Medieval Latin alembicum, from Arabic الإِنْبِيق (al-ʔinbīq, “distilling flask”) or الأَنْبِيق (al-ʔanbīq), from Ancient Greek ἄμβιξ (ámbix, “cup”).

parole.significato: syrup (a thick liquid with a high sugar content)
parole.testo: A wanderword. Via Medieval Latin siruppus, syrupus, from Arabic شَرَاب (šarāb, “a drink, beverage, wine, coffee, syrup”), from شَرِبَ (šariba, “to drink”). Compare German Sirup, French sirop, Italian sciroppo.
